summary.text: A binomial–Fibonacci identity gives \(2nS(n)=L_{2n}-1\), so integrality would imply \(2n\mid L_{2n}-1\); periodic congruences modulo \(4\) and \(5\) rule this out when \(n\) is even or divisible by \(3\) or \(5\). Otherwise, for the least prime factor \(p\ge7\) of \(n\), roots of \(x^2-x-1\) over a finite-field extension and a Frobenius/order argument force such a root to have order \(12\), whence the twelfth Lucas identity gives \(p\mid320\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac1i\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1},
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the denominator of \(S_n\) when the rational number is written in lowest terms with positive denominator. We prove that \(a(n)\ne1\) for every integer \(n>1\).

Write \(F_0=0,F_1=1\), and \(F_{r+2}=F_{r+1}+F_r\) for the Fibonacci numbers. We first express \(S_n\) in terms of Fibonacci numbers.

A standard combinatorial form of the Fibonacci numbers is
\[
F_{N+1}=\sum_{j\ge 0}\binom{N-j}{j}.
\tag{1}
\]
Here terms with \(j>N-j\) are zero, so the sum is finite. This identity follows directly by induction on \(N\), using Pascal's identity, or from the usual tiling interpretation of Fibonacci numbers.

Taking \(N=2n\) in (1), the nonzero indices are \(0\le j\le n\). Separating the term \(j=0\), which is \(1\), gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{2n-i}{i}=F_{2n+1}-1.
\tag{2}
\]
Taking \(N=2n-2\), and then writing \(j=i-1\), gives, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}=F_{2n-1}.
\tag{3}
\]
(The last possible term corresponds to \(j=n-1\).)

For \(1\le i\le n\), put
\[
A_i=\binom{2n-i}{i},\qquad B_i=\binom{2n-i-1}{i-1}.
\]
The elementary binomial identity
\[
(2n-i)B_i=iA_i
\]
implies
\[
2nB_i=i(A_i+B_i).
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the first equality is the usual relation
\(r\binom{r-1}{i-1}=i\binom ri\), with \(r=2n-i\), and adding \(iB_i\) to both sides gives (4). Divide (4) by \(i\) and sum over \(1\le i\le n\). By (2) and (3),
\[
2nS_n
 =\sum_{i=1}^n(A_i+B_i)
 =F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}-1.
\tag{5}
\]
Define
\[
M_n=F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}.
\]
Thus (5) says
\[
2nS_n=M_n-1.
\tag{6}
\]
The quantity \(M_n\) is the Lucas number \(L_{2n}\), but we will only use the displayed Fibonacci expression.

We next prove the number-theoretic assertion
\[
2n\nmid M_n-1\qquad(n>1).
\tag{7}
\]
We begin with two elementary congruence patterns.

The Fibonacci addition formula gives
\[
F_{k+6}=5F_k+8F_{k+1},
\]
so
\[
F_{k+6}\equiv F_k\pmod4.
\tag{8}
\]
Consequently, increasing \(n\) by \(3\) increases both indices \(2n+1\) and \(2n-1\) by \(6\), and hence
\[
M_{n+3}\equiv M_n\pmod4.
\]
The initial values are
\[
M_1=F_3+F_1=3,
\quad M_2=F_5+F_3=7\equiv3\pmod4,
\quad M_3=F_7+F_5=18\equiv2\pmod4.
\]
It follows that, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
M_n\equiv
\begin{cases}
2\pmod4,&3\mid n,\\
3\pmod4,&3\nmid n.
\end{cases}
\tag{9}
\]

We also need a congruence modulo \(5\). Set \(j=2n-1\). The addition formulas
\[
F_{j+6}=5F_j+8F_{j+1},\qquad
F_{j+4}=2F_j+3F_{j+1},\qquad
F_{j+2}=F_j+F_{j+1}
\]
show that
\[
F_{j+6}+F_{j+4}\equiv F_{j+2}+F_j\pmod5.
\]
Therefore
\[
M_{n+2}\equiv M_n\pmod5.
\]
For odd \(n\), repeated subtraction of \(2\) reduces to \(n=1\), and \(M_1=3\). Hence
\[
n\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M_n\equiv3\pmod5.
\tag{10}
\]

Suppose now, toward proving (7), that
\[
2n\mid M_n-1.
\tag{11}
\]
We first eliminate several cases.

If \(n\) is even, then \(4\mid2n\), so (11) implies \(M_n\equiv1\pmod4\). This contradicts (9), which says that \(M_n\) is congruent to either \(2\) or \(3\) modulo \(4\).

Thus \(n\) is odd. If \(3\mid n\), then (9) gives \(M_n\equiv2\pmod4\), so \(M_n-1\) is odd. But \(2\mid2n\), and (11) would make \(M_n-1\) even, a contradiction.

We may therefore assume that \(n\) is odd and \(3\nmid n\). If \(5\mid n\), then (11) implies \(5\mid M_n-1\), or \(M_n\equiv1\pmod5\). This contradicts (10). We are left with
\[
2\nmid n,\qquad3\nmid n,\qquad5\nmid n.
\tag{12}
\]

Let \(p\) be the smallest prime divisor of \(n\). Since \(n>1\), such a prime exists. By (12),
\[
p\ge7.
\tag{13}
\]
Moreover, (11) implies
\[
p\mid M_n-1.
\tag{14}
\]
We will show that (13) and (14) are impossible.

Work over a finite field \(K\) of characteristic \(p\) in which the polynomial
\[
x^2-x-1
\]
splits; for example, take its splitting field over \(\mathbf F_p\). Choose a root \(\alpha\in K\), and put
\[
\beta=1-\alpha.
\]
Then both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are roots and
\[
\alpha^2=\alpha+1,
\qquad \beta^2=\beta+1,
\qquad \alpha+\beta=1,
\qquad \alpha\beta=-1.
\tag{15}
\]
In particular, \(\alpha\ne0\).

For every \(k\ge0\), the following Lucas-power identity holds in \(K\):
\[
\alpha^k+\beta^k=2F_{k+1}-F_k.
\tag{16}
\]
To see this without using any analytic formula, note that both sides have initial values \(2\) at \(k=0\) and \(1\) at \(k=1\). Also, because each of \(\alpha,\beta\) satisfies \(x^2=x+1\), the left side obeys the Fibonacci recurrence in \(k\); the right side does as well. Thus induction proves (16).

For \(k=2n\), the Fibonacci recurrence gives
\[
2F_{2n+1}-F_{2n}
 =F_{2n+1}+F_{2n-1}=M_n.
\]
By (14), \(M_n=1\) in characteristic \(p\). Therefore (16) yields
\[
\alpha^{2n}+\beta^{2n}=1.
\tag{17}
\]
We now derive a contradiction from (17).

Let \(D\) be the multiplicative order of \(\alpha\) in the finite group \(K^\times\). We first constrain the prime divisors of \(D\). In characteristic \(p\), Frobenius preserves the equation defining \(\alpha\):
\[
(\alpha^p)^2=(\alpha^2)^p=(\alpha+1)^p=\alpha^p+1.
\]
Thus \(\alpha^p\) is another root of \(x^2-x-1\), so
\[
\alpha^p=\alpha\quad\text{or}\quad \alpha^p=\beta.
\tag{18}
\]
In the first case, cancellation of the nonzero element \(\alpha\) gives \(\alpha^{p-1}=1\), and hence
\[
D\mid p-1.
\tag{19}
\]
In the second case, using \(\alpha\beta=-1\),
\[
\alpha^{p+1}=\alpha^p\alpha=\beta\alpha=-1,
\]
so \(\alpha^{2(p+1)}=1\), and hence
\[
D\mid2(p+1).
\tag{20}
\]

Every prime divisor \(q\) of \(D\) is strictly less than \(p\). This is immediate from (19). Under (20), either \(q=2\), or \(q\mid p+1\). If \(q\ne2\), then \(q\) is odd. Since \(p\) is odd, \(p+1\) is even, so in a factorization \(p+1=qc\), the cofactor \(c\) must be even. Therefore \(2q\le p+1\), which, for \(p\ge7\), gives \(q<p\).

Because \(p\) is the smallest prime divisor of \(n\), every prime divisor of \(n\) is at least \(p\). No prime can consequently divide both \(D\) and \(n\). Thus
\[
\gcd(D,n)=1.
\tag{21}
\]

Set
\[
w=\alpha^{2n}.
\]
Since \(\alpha\beta=-1\) and \(2n\) is even,
\[
w\beta^{2n}=(\alpha\beta)^{2n}=1.
\tag{22}
\]
Together, (17) and (22) imply that \(w\) satisfies
\[
w^2-w+1=0.
\tag{23}
\]
Indeed, multiply (17) by \(w\) and use (22). Equation (23) gives
\[
w^3=-1,
\qquad w^6=1.
\tag{24}
\]
Also \(w\ne1\), since substituting \(w=1\) into (23) would give \(1=0\).

We claim that \(w\) has order exactly \(6\). Its order divides \(6\) by (24). It is not \(1\). It cannot be \(3\), because \(w^3=-1\ne1\) in characteristic \(p\ge7\). It cannot be \(2\): if \(w^2=1\), subtracting (23) gives \(w=2\), and substituting this into (23) gives \(3=0\), again impossible in characteristic at least \(7\). Thus its order is \(6\).

For an element of order \(D\), the order of its \(r\)-th power is
\[
\frac{D}{\gcd(D,r)}.
\]
Applying this with \(r=2n\) gives
\[
6=\frac{D}{\gcd(D,2n)}.
\tag{25}
\]
Let \(g=\gcd(D,2n)\). Equation (25) gives \(D=6g\), so in particular \(2\mid D\). From (21), \(D\) is coprime to \(n\). Since \(g\mid D\) and \(g\mid2n\), it follows that \(g\mid2\). On the other hand, \(2\mid D\) and \(2\mid2n\), so \(2\mid g\). Hence
\[
g=2,
\qquad D=12.
\tag{26}
\]
Therefore \(\alpha^{12}=1\). Since \(\alpha\beta=-1\), raising to the twelfth power also shows \(\beta^{12}=1\). Taking \(k=12\) in (16), we consequently obtain, in \(K\),
\[
2F_{13}-F_{12}=2.
\]
But \(F_{12}=144\) and \(F_{13}=233\), so the left side is
\[
2\cdot233-144=322.
\]
Thus \(322=2\) in characteristic \(p\), which means
\[
p\mid320=2^6\cdot5.
\]
As \(p\) is prime, this forces \(p=2\) or \(p=5\), contradicting \(p\ge7\). This contradiction completes the remaining case and proves (7):
\[
2n\nmid M_n-1\quad\text{for every }n>1.
\]

Finally, suppose for contradiction that \(a(n)=1\). A rational number in lowest terms has denominator \(1\) exactly when it is an integer, so \(S_n\in\mathbb Z\). Equation (6) would then give
\[
M_n-1=2nS_n,
\]
and therefore \(2n\mid M_n-1\). This contradicts (7). Hence the denominator of \(S_n\) is not \(1\) for every \(n>1\), as required.
